questions.stem: A 34 year old man of Maltese descent has a blood test before donating blood. He feels well and has no gastrointestinal symptoms. Examination is normal. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A well Mediterranean man with a very low MCV, a near-normal Hb, normal ferritin and HbA2 above 3.5% has beta-thalassaemia trait.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Mediterranean ethnicity, no symptoms, MCV much lower than the Hb would suggest, normal ferritin, HbA2 above 3.5%.

elim: Alpha trait gives a normal HbA2 on electrophoresis; here HbA2 is raised.
He has no chronic illness and the MCV is far too low for the mild drop in Hb.
Ferritin is normal, and iron deficiency does not raise HbA2.
Rare, usually with high ferritin, and does not raise HbA2.

steps.x: **C. Beta-thalassaemia trait.** Disproportionate microcytosis + normal ferritin + HbA2 >3.5% = beta-thalassaemia trait.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man originally from Thailand has a full blood count before a hernia repair. He is well and eats a mixed diet. He has no blood loss. A blood film shows microcytic red cells with basophilic stippling. Haemoglobin electrophoresis is normal. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A Southeast Asian patient with microcytic anaemia, normal ferritin and a NORMAL electrophoresis has alpha-thalassaemia trait; beta trait would raise HbA2.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Southeast Asian background, microcytosis, normal iron stores and a normal electrophoresis.

elim: Beta trait raises HbA2 above 3.5%; electrophoresis here is normal.
Ferritin is normal and he has no blood loss or poor diet.
Can cause basophilic stippling, but he has no exposure, abdominal pain or neuropathy.
This would show HbS on electrophoresis and is not microcytic.

steps.x: **A. Alpha-thalassaemia trait.** Microcytic + normal ferritin + normal electrophoresis in a Southeast Asian patient = alpha-thalassaemia trait.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman from Laos has a 22 week anomaly scan. The fetus has gross skin oedema, ascites, pleural effusions and cardiomegaly. She and her partner both have alpha-thalassaemia trait with deletions of both alpha genes on one chromosome. She is rhesus positive and parvovirus B19 IgM is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Two parents each carrying both alpha deletions on one chromosome can have a fetus with all 4 alpha genes deleted; gamma chains form HbBart's and the fetus becomes hydropic.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Both parents carry alpha deletions; the fetus is hydropic in utero with infection and rhesus excluded.

elim: Fetal HbF needs no beta chains, so beta-thalassaemia major presents after birth, not in utero.
A classic cause of hydrops, but the IgM is negative.
The mother is rhesus positive.
Causes cystic hygroma and lymphoedema, and is not linked to the parents' alpha trait.

steps.x: **A. Bart's hydrops fetalis.** All 4 alpha genes deleted = HbBart's (4 gamma chains) = hydrops fetalis, incompatible with life.

questions.stem: A 9 month old boy of Cypriot descent is pale and breathless on feeding. He has a full abdomen with a palpable liver and spleen. His pulse rate is 168 bpm. Haemoglobin electrophoresis shows no HbA. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Severe microcytic anaemia, hepatosplenomegaly and tachycardia in the first year with no HbA and raised HbF and HbA2 is homozygous beta-thalassaemia major.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: 9 month old boy of Cypriot descent
steps.x: Mediterranean infant, under 2, severe anaemia, hepatosplenomegaly, no HbA and compensatory HbF.

elim: Trait is mild and asymptomatic, with a normal electrophoresis.
Heterozygotes are well with mild anaemia and still make HbA.
Does not abolish HbA or cause hepatosplenomegaly.
Electrophoresis would show HbS, and the anaemia is normocytic.

steps.x: **B. Beta-thalassaemia major.** No beta chains = no HbA; HbF and HbA2 compensate but not enough: beta-thalassaemia major.

questions.stem: An 18 month old boy of Ghanaian descent has had painful, swollen fingers on both hands for 2 days and cries when they are touched. His sclerae are yellow. His temperature is 37.4°C and pulse rate 134 bpm. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A young child of African descent with painful swollen fingers (dactylitis), jaundice and a haemolytic picture has sickle cell disease.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: painful, swollen fingers on both hands
steps.x: African ancestry, childhood onset, pain from vaso-occlusion, jaundice and haemolytic anaemia.

elim: Microcytic anaemia with failure to thrive, not painful swollen digits with haemolysis.
Causes haemolysis and jaundice but not painful vaso-occlusive swelling of the hands.
Does not cause anaemia with reticulocytosis and jaundice.
Rarely symmetrical in both hands; he is nearly afebrile.

steps.x: **E. Sickle cell disease.** Pain + haemolytic anaemia + jaundice in a child of African descent = sickle cell disease.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man of Nigerian descent is given ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection. Three days later he has dark urine, yellow sclerae and breathlessness on exertion. A blood film shows bite cells and polychromasia. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Acute haemolysis after a quinolone with bite cells and polychromasia on the film is G6PD deficiency.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
A quinolone trigger, then sudden haemolysis with bite cells.

elim: Causes isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia without anaemia or bite cells.
The film would show spherocytes, and the haemolysis is not drug-triggered.
Would present in childhood with pain and sickle cells on the film.
Shows spherocytes and a positive direct antiglobulin test, not bite cells.

steps.x: **A. G6PD deficiency.** Oxidant drug + acute haemolysis + bite cells = G6PD deficiency.

questions.stem: A 15 year old girl with sickle cell disease is admitted with a painful crisis in her legs. On day 2 she develops a cough and left-sided chest pain. Her temperature is 38.1°C, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray, day 2
visual.caption: New left lower zone consolidation in a sickle cell patient: acute chest syndrome.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Chest pain, fever, hypoxia and a new infiltrate in a patient with sickle cell is acute chest syndrome, a medical emergency.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Sickle cell, a painful crisis, then chest symptoms, hypoxia and new consolidation.

elim: The X-ray shows consolidation, not a lung edge.
There is no cardiac history and the change is one-sided consolidation.
Gives a usually clear X-ray; a new infiltrate in sickle cell is acute chest syndrome.
No trauma, and it does not cause hypoxia with a new infiltrate.

steps.x: **A. Acute chest syndrome.** Sickle cell + chest pain/breathlessness + new infiltrate = acute chest syndrome.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman with sickle cell disease stopped taking her penicillin V a year ago. She now has a 12 hour history of fever and confusion. Her temperature is 39.6°C, pulse rate 128 bpm and BP 84/50 mmHg. Blood cultures grow Streptococcus pneumoniae. Her spleen is not palpable.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying reason for this infection?
questions.e: Repeated splenic infarction leaves sickle cell patients functionally asplenic, so encapsulated organisms like pneumococcus cause overwhelming sepsis; hence lifelong penicillin and vaccination.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Encapsulated organism, overwhelming sepsis, off prophylaxis, impalpable spleen.

elim: Sickle cell causes haemolysis with an active marrow, not marrow failure.
Not a feature of sickle cell disease.
Not the reason for overwhelming pneumococcal sepsis.
Sickle cell does not cause neutropenia; the spleen is the problem.

steps.x: **B. Functional hyposplenism.** Sickle cell destroys the spleen by infarction: hyposplenism, so prophylactic penicillin and vaccines.

questions.stem: A 31 year old man with beta-thalassaemia major has had fortnightly transfusions since infancy. He has not taken chelation for years. He has reddish-brown macules over both shins, easy bruising and dark, bronzed skin. His second and third MCP joints ache. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of these findings?
questions.e: Years of transfusion without chelation cause iron overload: haemosiderin in the skin of the legs, bronzing, bruising and MCP arthropathy.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Lifelong transfusions, no chelation, skin pigmentation, leg macules, MCP pain, very high ferritin.

elim: Does not cause bronzed skin or a ferritin this high.
Iron overload, not RA, explains MCP arthropathy with skin pigmentation here.
Causes bruising and perifollicular haemorrhages, but not bronzed skin or a high ferritin.
Does not cause joint pain, bronzing or a very high ferritin.

steps.x: **D. Transfusional haemosiderosis.** Transfusions without chelation = haemosiderosis (skin, joints, heart, liver, pancreas).

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman of Greek descent is planning a pregnancy. Her brother was recently told he has beta-thalassaemia trait. She feels well, has light periods and eats meat. Examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely result of her full blood count if she also carries the trait?
questions.e: Thalassaemia trait gives a very low MCV with only a slightly low Hb: the MCV is disproportionately low for the Hb.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Mediterranean, family history of trait, asymptomatic.

elim: A normal count; the trait gives microcytosis.
A severe normocytic anaemia does not fit an asymptomatic carrier.
A modest MCV fall with a large Hb fall is typical of iron deficiency, not trait.
Macrocytosis suggests B12 or folate deficiency.

steps.x: **A. Hb 116 g/L, MCV 63 fL.** Trait = MCV disproportionately low compared with the Hb.

questions.stem: An 11 month old girl of Italian descent has been pale and irritable for 3 months and has dropped from the 50th to the 9th weight centile. Her haemoglobin is 61 g/L (100–140) with an MCV of 57 fL (70–86). Haemoglobin electrophoresis shows absent HbA.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
questions.e: Beta-thalassaemia major presents before age 2 with anaemia, failure to thrive and hepatosplenomegaly from extramedullary haemopoiesis and haemolysis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: 11 month old girl of Italian descent
dropped from the 50th to the 9th weight centile
steps.x: An infant under 2 with severe microcytic anaemia, failure to thrive and no HbA.

elim: Not a feature of thalassaemia; think cyanotic heart or lung disease.
Suggests infection or leukaemia, not thalassaemia.
A sign of chronic iron deficiency, not of thalassaemia major.
A sign of liver disease or pregnancy.

steps.x: **C. Hepatosplenomegaly.** Thalassaemia major in infancy = anaemia + failure to thrive + hepatosplenomegaly.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman with sickle cell disease has had severe pain in her lower back and thighs for 12 hours after a long run on a hot day. Her temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 122/74 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Her chest is clear and her spleen is not palpable. Her Hb is at her usual level.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Severe bone pain after dehydration, with normal oxygen, a clear chest and a stable Hb, is a vaso-occlusive (painful) crisis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: long run on a hot day
steps.x: Dehydration trigger, bony pain, no chest signs, normal sats, stable Hb.

elim: She has no chest pain, no hypoxia and a clear chest.
The Hb would fall sharply with low reticulocytes; hers is at baseline.
Multifocal pain after dehydration with no fever fits vaso-occlusion.
Causes a rapidly enlarging spleen and a falling Hb, mainly in children.

steps.x: **E. Vaso-occlusive crisis.** Sickle cell + dehydration + bone pain, nothing else = vaso-occlusive crisis.

questions.stem: A 6 year old boy of Iraqi descent is brought in with tiredness and dark red urine. He had a febrile viral illness 3 days ago, treated with paracetamol only. His conjunctivae are pale and his sclerae yellow. His Hb is 79 g/L (115–155) and reticulocytes 7% (0.5–2.5). His direct antiglobulin test is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on his blood film?
questions.e: Acute haemolysis after an intercurrent illness in a Middle Eastern boy suggests G6PD deficiency: oxidised haemoglobin is removed by the spleen, leaving bite cells.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Middle Eastern boy, intercurrent illness trigger, acute DAT-negative haemolysis.

elim: Seen in B12 or folate deficiency.
Seen in iron deficiency.
Seen in hereditary spherocytosis or autoimmune haemolysis; his DAT is negative.
Seen in thalassaemia and liver disease, not acute oxidative haemolysis.

steps.x: **A. Bite cells.** G6PD deficiency = bite cells, reticulocytosis and polychromasia.

questions.stem: A 3 year old girl of Nigerian descent has had two episodes of severe limb pain needing admission. She is mildly jaundiced. Her Hb is 78 g/L (110–140), MCV 82 fL (75–87) and reticulocytes 9% (0.5–2.5). A sickle solubility test is positive.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Haemoglobin electrophoresis is the gold standard: it separates HbS from HbA and HbF and distinguishes sickle cell disease from trait.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or confirm before reading the options.

clues: two episodes of severe limb pain
steps.x: A haemolytic picture with pain crises and a positive screening test, which needs confirmation.

elim: May show sickle cells but does not define the haemoglobin type.
Not needed; this is a haemoglobin structure problem.
Tests for immune haemolysis, not abnormal haemoglobin.
It is positive in both trait and disease, so it cannot confirm sickle cell disease.

steps.x: **D. Haemoglobin electrophoresis.** Confirming any haemoglobinopathy = haemoglobin electrophoresis (gold standard).

questions.stem: A 4 year old boy of Greek descent is brought to the GP because he looks pale and tires easily. He eats well. There is no jaundice and no organomegaly. His father was told he had 'a blood trait' at school.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: First-line is the FBC: thalassaemia gives a microcytic pattern, which then leads to ferritin and electrophoresis.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or confirm before reading the options.
Pallor and tiredness in a Mediterranean child with a family trait.

elim: Invasive and not a first step for a pale, well child.
The confirmatory test, done after the FBC shows microcytosis.
Not the first test; the FBC indices guide what comes next.
No organomegaly, and it does not diagnose anaemia.

steps.x: **C. Full blood count.** First-line = FBC (microcytic in thalassaemia, haemolytic in sickle cell); electrophoresis confirms.

questions.stem: A 7 month old boy of Turkish descent has severe pallor, poor feeding and splenomegaly. His Hb is 55 g/L (100–140) and MCV 58 fL (70–86). His parents both have thalassaemia trait. Haemoglobin electrophoresis is sent.
questions.q: Which is the most likely electrophoresis result?
o: No HbA, with raised HbF and HbA2
questions.e: Beta-thalassaemia major makes no beta chains, so there is no HbA; HbF (and HbA2) rise to compensate.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or confirm before reading the options.

clues: 7 month old boy of Turkish descent
steps.x: Two carrier parents, a severely anaemic microcytic infant: homozygous beta-thalassaemia major.

elim: This is sickle cell disease.
Fits alpha-thalassaemia trait, not a severely anaemic infant.
This is beta-thalassaemia trait, an asymptomatic carrier state.
There is no beta-chain production, so no HbA can be made.

steps.x: **B. No HbA, with raised HbF and HbA2.** Beta-thalassaemia major on electrophoresis = no HbA, raised HbF and HbA2.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman originally from the Philippines is found to have a Hb of 106 g/L (115–165) and an MCV of 69 fL (80–100) on a routine blood test. She has normal periods and no gastrointestinal symptoms. She feels well.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: A microcytic anaemia needs ferritin first: a normal ferritin in a Southeast Asian woman points to alpha-thalassaemia trait.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or confirm before reading the options.
Southeast Asian woman, mild microcytic anaemia, no blood loss, well.

elim: Far too invasive for a mild microcytic anaemia in a well woman.
Only if iron deficiency is confirmed and unexplained.
For immune haemolysis, which causes a normal or high MCV.
Folate deficiency causes macrocytosis.

steps.x: **D. Serum ferritin.** Microcytic anaemia: ferritin first; normal ferritin + normal electrophoresis = alpha-thalassaemia trait.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man of Sardinian descent had an episode of dark urine and jaundice after starting primaquine for malaria. His blood film at the time showed bite cells. He has recovered fully and attends clinic 3 months later.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Haemolysis after primaquine with bite cells suggests G6PD deficiency; measure the enzyme once recovered, since young red cells can give a falsely normal level during haemolysis.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or confirm before reading the options.
Mediterranean man, oxidant drug trigger, bite cells, now recovered.

elim: Tests for autoimmune haemolysis; the trigger and bite cells point to G6PD.
Diagnoses structural haemoglobin disorders, not enzyme deficiency.
Used for hereditary spherocytosis.
Screens for HbS.

steps.x: **B. G6PD enzyme assay.** Suspected G6PD deficiency = G6PD enzyme assay, done after the acute episode.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man with sickle cell disease has had pain in his ribs and back for 1 day. He now feels breathless and has right-sided chest pain on breathing in. His temperature is 38.0°C, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. There are crackles at the right base.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Chest pain, breathlessness and hypoxia in sickle cell suggest acute chest syndrome; the chest X-ray shows the new infiltrate.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or confirm before reading the options.

clues: breathless and has right-sided chest pain
steps.x: Sickle cell with chest pain, fever, hypoxia and crackles: suspect acute chest syndrome.

elim: Not first; acute chest syndrome must be looked for on a chest X-ray.
Non-specific and often raised in a sickle crisis.
Does not show the lung infiltrate that defines acute chest syndrome.
Has no role in an acutely hypoxic patient.

steps.x: **A. Chest X-ray.** Suspected acute chest syndrome = chest X-ray for a new infiltrate (emergency).

questions.stem: A 9 year old boy with sickle cell disease has severe pain in both knees and his lower back after a cold, wet football match. He scores the pain 9 out of 10. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 108/66 mmHg and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. His mucous membranes are dry. His chest is clear.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Oxygen, IV fluids and IV morphine
questions.e: An acute sickle crisis is treated with oxygen (sats are low), IV fluids (he is dry) and prompt strong analgesia.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Severe pain, low sats and dehydration in a vaso-occlusive crisis.

elim: Kept for acute chest syndrome or stroke, not an uncomplicated painful crisis.
An iron chelator for transfusion overload; it does not treat a crisis.
Long-term prevention of crises, not acute treatment.
Pain of 9 out of 10 with hypoxia and dehydration needs admission and strong analgesia.

steps.x: **E. Oxygen, IV fluids and IV morphine.** Sickle crisis = oxygen + IV fluids + analgesia, fast.

questions.stem: A 3 month old girl was diagnosed with sickle cell disease on newborn screening, confirmed by haemoglobin electrophoresis. She is well and feeding normally. Her parents ask what she needs now to prevent life-threatening infection.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term measure?
questions.e: Splenic dysfunction makes children with sickle cell vulnerable to pneumococcal sepsis, so they take prophylactic penicillin and have full vaccination.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.

clues: sickle cell disease on newborn screening
steps.x: A well infant with sickle cell: think splenic dysfunction and encapsulated organisms.

elim: Only for iron overload from repeated transfusion.
This is the treatment for beta-thalassaemia major.
Not indicated; sickle cell anaemia is haemolytic, not iron deficient.
The spleen is already failing; removing it does not prevent infection.

steps.x: **D. Phenoxymethylpenicillin prophylaxis.** Sickle cell long-term = prophylactic antibiotics + vaccination (+ hydroxyurea).

questions.stem: A 13 month old boy of Lebanese descent has just been diagnosed with beta-thalassaemia major. He has a Hb of 59 g/L (100–140), failure to thrive and splenomegaly. His parents ask how often he will need treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate transfusion plan?
questions.e: With no beta chains, HbF and HbA2 cannot compensate, so beta-thalassaemia major needs lifelong transfusions about every fortnight.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.

clues: how often he will need treatment
steps.x: Transfusion-dependent thalassaemia diagnosed in infancy.

elim: Far too infrequent to suppress his own ineffective marrow.
Episodic transfusion leaves him anaemic, growth-failing and deformed.
He is not iron deficient; oral iron worsens overload.
HbF compensation is never enough in thalassaemia major.

steps.x: **D. Transfusion every 2 weeks for life.** Beta-thalassaemia major = lifelong fortnightly transfusions plus chelation.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman of Cypriot descent was started on ferrous sulfate 3 months ago for a microcytic anaemia. Her Hb has not changed. She feels well. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Stop iron and offer partner testing
questions.e: A raised HbA2 with normal ferritin is beta-thalassaemia trait: no treatment, stop the iron, and test the partner for the risk of an affected child.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Microcytosis that did not respond to iron, normal ferritin, HbA2 above 3.5%.

elim: She is not iron deficient; more iron risks overload.
Her ferritin is normal, so there is no iron deficiency to explain.
Trait carriers are not transfused and do not need chelation.
Trait is mild and asymptomatic; transfusion is for thalassaemia major.

steps.x: **E. Stop iron and offer partner testing.** Beta-thalassaemia trait = no treatment; stop iron and offer partner screening.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man with beta-thalassaemia major has transfusions every 2 weeks. He is well but his liver MRI shows iron deposition. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment for his iron?
questions.e: Regular transfusions cause iron overload, which is treated with iron chelation using desferrioxamine; venesection is impossible in severe anaemia.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Transfusion-dependent, rising ferritin, iron in the liver.

elim: Raises HbF in sickle cell disease; it does not remove iron.
A copper chelator used in Wilson's disease.
Removes iron in haemochromatosis but would worsen his anaemia.
Does not remove iron and can increase iron toxicity.

steps.x: **A. Desferrioxamine.** Transfusional iron overload = chelation with desferrioxamine.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man has G6PD deficiency confirmed on enzyme assay after an episode of haemolysis. He is well now. He asks which medicines he should avoid in future. His GP is reviewing his repeat prescriptions.
questions.q: Which medication is most important for him to avoid?
questions.e: Dapsone is a potent oxidant that triggers haemolysis in G6PD deficiency, as do primaquine, sulfa drugs, nitrofurantoin, quinolones and fava beans.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Known G6PD deficiency: avoid oxidant drugs.

elim: Safe in G6PD deficiency.
Not an oxidant trigger.
Not an oxidant trigger.
Safe at normal doses.

steps.x: **C. Dapsone.** G6PD triggers: fava beans, primaquine, dapsone, sulfa drugs, nitrofurantoin, quinolones, high-dose aspirin.

questions.stem: A 20 year old woman with sickle cell disease asks what is wrong with her haemoglobin. Electrophoresis showed HbS 88%, HbF 9% and HbA2 3%, with no HbA. Her parents both have sickle cell trait.
questions.q: Which is the most likely genetic mechanism?
o: Deletion of all four alpha-globin genes
Point mutation in the beta-globin gene
Reduced synthesis of normal beta chains
questions.e: HbS results from a single point mutation in the beta-globin gene (glutamic acid to valine), giving a structurally abnormal haemoglobin.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the vignette.
Abnormal haemoglobin S from two carrier parents.

elim: This causes HbBart's hydrops fetalis.
Causes an enzyme deficiency, not abnormal haemoglobin.
This is beta-thalassaemia: less globin, not abnormal globin.
Causes conditions such as Huntington's disease.

steps.x: **C. Point mutation in the beta-globin gene.** Sickle cell = point mutation in beta-globin (HbS): a structural haemoglobinopathy.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man with sickle cell disease has had a deep ache in his right hip for 6 weeks, worse on walking. He is afebrile. An MRI shows avascular necrosis of the right femoral head.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his hip disease?
o: Occlusion of small vessels by rigid sickled cells
questions.e: Rigid sickled red cells block small vessels, causing ischaemia; in the femoral head this produces avascular necrosis.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the vignette.

clues: avascular necrosis of the right femoral head
steps.x: Sickle cell with bone death from lost blood supply.

elim: He is afebrile with avascular necrosis, not osteomyelitis.
Transfusional arthropathy affects the MCP joints, not femoral head necrosis.
This explains skeletal deformity in thalassaemia.
No steroid use is described.

steps.x: **D. Occlusion of small vessels by rigid sickled cells.** Sickled cells occlude small vessels = vaso-occlusion and end-organ ischaemia.

questions.stem: A 12 year old boy with beta-thalassaemia major moved to the UK last year and was poorly transfused before then. He has frontal bossing and an overgrown upper jaw. Skull X-ray shows a 'hair-on-end' appearance.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his skull changes?
o: Compensatory expansion of the bone marrow
questions.e: Ineffective erythropoiesis drives massive compensatory marrow expansion, widening the skull and facial bones; regular transfusion suppresses it.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the vignette.
Under-transfused thalassaemia major with skull and facial bone overgrowth.

elim: This is multiple myeloma's lytic lesions.
Iron overload damages organs, not the shape of the skull.
This is rickets or osteomalacia.
Vaso-occlusion is the mechanism in sickle cell disease.

steps.x: **B. Compensatory expansion of the bone marrow.** Thalassaemia bone deformity = marrow expansion driven by ineffective erythropoiesis.

questions.stem: A 16 year old girl with beta-thalassaemia major asks why her bone marrow is very active but she is still anaemic. A marrow sample taken at diagnosis showed marked erythroid hyperplasia. Her reticulocyte count was inappropriately low.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her anaemia?
o: Lack of iron for haem synthesis
Unpaired alpha chains precipitating in red cell precursors
questions.e: With no beta chains, excess unpaired alpha chains precipitate in red cell precursors, which die in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis) or are haemolysed.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the vignette.

clues: very active but she is still anaemic
steps.x: A busy marrow that fails to deliver red cells: ineffective erythropoiesis.

elim: This is autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.
Her marrow is hyperplastic, so the drive is present.
Thalassaemia is a globin chain problem, not iron lack.
This is the mechanism of sickle cell disease.

steps.x: **E. Unpaired alpha chains precipitating in red cell precursors.** Thalassaemia anaemia = chain imbalance, precipitated chains, ineffective erythropoiesis and haemolysis.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man of Saudi descent develops haemolysis 2 days after taking a sulfonamide antibiotic. His blood film shows bite cells. He is found to have G6PD deficiency.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his haemolysis?
o: Abnormal spectrin in the red cell membrane
Reduced NADPH, so glutathione cannot protect against oxidants
questions.e: G6PD makes NADPH in the pentose phosphate pathway; without it glutathione stays oxidised, so oxidant drugs damage haemoglobin and the cells haemolyse.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the vignette.
An oxidant drug in G6PD deficiency.

elim: This is hereditary spherocytosis.
This is autoimmune haemolysis, with a positive DAT.
This is sickle cell disease.
This is thalassaemia.

steps.x: **E. Reduced NADPH, so glutathione cannot protect against oxidants.** G6PD deficiency = low NADPH = low reduced glutathione = oxidative haemolysis.

questions.stem: A couple of Greek descent attend antenatal counselling. Both have beta-thalassaemia trait confirmed by a raised HbA2. They are well. Their first child is unaffected. They ask about the risk for their next pregnancy.
questions.q: Which is the chance that their next child has beta-thalassaemia major?
questions.e: Thalassaemia is autosomal recessive: two carriers have a 1 in 4 chance of a homozygous (major) child each pregnancy.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the vignette.
Two heterozygous carriers of an autosomal recessive disorder.

steps.x: **B. 1 in 4.** Two carriers = 1 in 4 affected, 1 in 2 carrier, 1 in 4 unaffected, each pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman with beta-thalassaemia major has had about 600 units of blood transfused over her life. She has developed heart failure and diabetes. Her ferritin is 6200 µg/L (30–400). Cardiac MRI shows myocardial iron.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her iron overload?
o: Increased gut absorption caused by a HFE mutation
Iron supplements given with her transfusions
The body has no way to excrete excess iron
questions.e: Each unit carries about 200 mg iron and the body has no regulated excretion route, so iron accumulates in heart, liver, pancreas and joints.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the vignette.
Lifelong transfusions, damage to heart and pancreas, very high ferritin.

Chelation removes iron; it does not add it.
Thalassaemia major patients are not given iron.
Platelets carry very little iron; red cells carry it.

steps.x: **E. The body has no way to excrete excess iron.** Transfusion iron enters faster than the body can lose it = haemosiderosis, so chelate.

questions.stem: A 6 month old boy of Maltese descent was well at birth but over the last 2 months has become pale and irritable, and his abdomen has become full. Haemoglobin electrophoresis shows no HbA.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason his symptoms began only after the first few months of life?
o: Switch from fetal to adult haemoglobin
questions.e: Before birth and in early infancy HbF (alpha2 gamma2) needs no beta chains; as gamma production falls and beta should take over, beta-thalassaemia major is unmasked.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the vignette.
Normal at birth, then anaemic at a few months, with no HbA.

Explains infections, not severe anaemia with no HbA.
He has not been transfused.
Diet does not change globin production.

steps.x: **E. Switch from fetal to adult haemoglobin.** Beta-thalassaemia major appears as HbF falls in the first year of life.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man with sickle cell disease has had four painful crises and one episode of acute chest syndrome in a year. He starts hydroxyurea. At 6 months he has had no crises.
questions.q: Which laboratory change best explains his improvement?
questions.e: Hydroxyurea increases fetal haemoglobin, which interferes with HbS polymerisation and so reduces vaso-occlusive crises.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the vignette.
Frequent crises, then fewer on hydroxyurea.

elim: Hydroxyurea is not an iron chelator.
HbA2 is not the protective haemoglobin.
More HbS would make crises worse.
Hydroxyurea can lower, not raise, platelets; it is not the mechanism.

steps.x: **C. Rise in HbF percentage.** Hydroxyurea raises HbF, which blocks HbS polymerisation = fewer crises.
